7090: The word gondola refers to several distinct things in English, but there's a quiet thread connecting most of them: a container or compartment that is carried, suspended, or floated. Once you see that thread, the word becomes much easier to remember across all its uses.
1. The Venetian Boat (The Most Famous Meaning)

When most people hear "gondola," they picture this: a long, narrow, flat-bottomed boat that glides through the canals of Venice, Italy. It has a distinctive curved shape — the front and back both rise upward in a graceful arc, and the boat is slightly asymmetrical (one side is a little wider than the other), which helps it move in a straight line when pushed from just one side.A gondola is steered and propelled by a single person called a gondolier, who stands at the rear (back) of the boat and pushes through the water using a long oar. The oar rests in a special wooden bracket on the side of the boat — the gondolier doesn't paddle alternately from side to side like a canoe; instead, they use a sweeping, twisting motion from one fixed position.

Gondolas are traditionally painted black (this became a rule centuries ago to prevent wealthy families from competing with each other through flashy decorations). They typically have a decorative metal ornament at the front called a ferro — a comb-like piece of metal whose six prongs are said by some to represent the six districts of Venice.

Today, gondolas in Venice are primarily used for tourist rides, though they were once the main everyday transport for Venetians, before motorboats took over.
2. The Cable Car Cabin (Very Common in Modern Use)

This is probably the second most common meaning you'll encounter. A gondola is the enclosed, cabin-like compartment that hangs from a cable and carries passengers up and down mountains or across valleys. You see these at ski resorts, mountain tourist attractions, and even some cities.The cabin itself is what's called the gondola — not the whole cable system, just the box or pod that hangs from the cable and travels along it. These gondolas are usually fully enclosed (with windows and a door), can carry several passengers at once, and are attached to the moving cable overhead. They travel continuously or in a loop, picking up and dropping off passengers at stations.

You might also hear these called cable cars, aerial trams, or ropeways, but when someone specifically says "gondola" in this context, they mean the hanging passenger cabin — the compartment itself.

When a hot air balloon floats through the sky, the people inside are not standing in the balloon itself — they're standing in a basket or compartment that hangs below the balloon. That basket is called a gondola.

The same word is used for the passenger compartment beneath a blimp or airship (like the Goodyear Blimp) — the enclosed cabin that hangs underneath the gas-filled envelope where pilots and passengers sit.

In both cases, the gondola is the habitable part — where humans are — suspended beneath the lifting part (the balloon or the gas bag).

In the world of railways and freight transport, a gondola (also called a gondola car or gondola railcar) is a type of freight wagon — a long, flat-bottomed, open-top railcar with low walls on the sides and ends.

Think of it like a big rectangular tub on wheels. Because the top is completely open, it's used to carry loose bulk materials that don't need protection from the weather: things like coal, gravel, scrap metal, sand, or ore. You load them in from the top with a crane or conveyor, and you can unload them by tipping the car or using machinery.

This type of railcar is extremely common in freight rail networks, particularly in North America.

Walk into almost any supermarket or large retail store, and look at the freestanding shelf units that run down the middle of the aisles — the ones you can access from both sides. In the retail and merchandising industry, those double-sided shelving structures are called gondolas (or gondola shelving).A gondola in a store consists of a central upright frame with adjustable shelves extending outward on both sides. Store managers talk about things like "end-cap gondolas" (the shelves at the end of an aisle, which are especially valuable display spots) and use the word routinely when planning store layouts. This meaning of the word is mostly used by people in the retail and grocery industries, not everyday shoppers — but you will encounter it if you ever work in retail or read about store design.

Here's a simple way to hold all of this in your head:

  • Venice → the iconic long black boat gliding through canals
  • Mountains / ski resorts → the enclosed cabin hanging from a cable overhead
  • Hot air balloons / blimps → the basket or cabin hanging below the balloon
  • Railways → the open-top freight wagon used to carry bulk cargo
  • Supermarkets → the double-sided freestanding shelf units in store aisles

The first three share a genuine conceptual link: in each, the gondola is a compartment that is either floating on water or suspended in the air, carrying people or goods. The freight railcar and the retail shelving share the shape — a flat-bottomed, open, tub-like structure — with the Venetian boat. That's why the same word stretched to cover all of these over time.

In everyday life, you're most likely to encounter "gondola" meaning the Venetian boat, the cable car cabin, or (if you're in the retail industry) the store shelving.
7091:
"Gone are the days" means that a certain time, era, or situation that once existed no longer exists. It is a way of saying that something which used to be true, common, or normal in the past has now ended — it belongs to history, not to the present.

Think of it like pointing to the past and saying: "That time is over. It doesn't happen anymore."
Breaking Down the Words

The expression is beautifully simple when you look at it word by word.

"Gone" means disappeared, finished, or no longer here. When something is gone, it has left and is not coming back — or at least, it is not here now.

"The days" refers to a period of time — not just one 24-hour day, but an entire era or phase in life when things were a certain way.

Put them together: "Gone are the days" = "Those times have disappeared."
Why Is the Word Order Reversed?

If you look at this phrase carefully, you will notice something unusual. In normal English, we say:

"The days are gone." — Subject (The days) → Verb (are gone)

But in this expression, the order is flipped:

"Gone are the days." — Verb first (Gone) → Subject after (the days)

This reversal is called inversion, and it is done deliberately. In English, when you bring a word to the very front of a sentence, it gets extra emphasis and dramatic weight. By placing "gone" at the very beginning, the speaker puts full emotional focus on the fact that something has ended. It makes the sentence feel more powerful, poetic, and expressive than simply saying "the days are gone."

This is why you will often see this expression in speeches, literature, song lyrics, and emotional conversations — places where people want their words to carry more feeling.
What Comes After the Expression

The expression is almost never used alone. It is typically followed by one of two things:

1. "When" + a description of what used to happen

This is the most common pattern. You describe the past situation after the word "when."

  • "Gone are the days when people had to visit a library to find information."
  • "Gone are the days when children played outside from morning until dark."
  • "Gone are the days when a letter took two weeks to arrive."

2. "Of" + a noun

Here, instead of a full sentence, you use a noun (a thing or idea) to describe what has ended.

  • "Gone are the days of affordable housing."
  • "Gone are the days of simple, quiet mornings."
  • "Gone are the days of trust between neighbors."

Both patterns work perfectly. Choose "when" when you want to describe an action or situation. Choose "of" when you want to refer to a concept, a thing, or a general era.
The Tone and Emotion Behind It

One of the most interesting things about this expression is that it can carry very different emotions depending on the speaker and the situation. The words themselves are neutral, but the context gives them their feeling.

Nostalgia and Wistfulness — This is the most common tone. The speaker misses the old days and feels a gentle sadness that they are over.

"Gone are the days when the whole family would gather around one radio to listen together." — Here, the speaker clearly misses that warmth and togetherness.

Relief and Gladness — Sometimes the speaker is happy that those days are gone, because the past was difficult, unjust, or inconvenient.

"Gone are the days when women were not allowed to vote." — Here, the tone is one of progress and relief.

"Gone are the days when I had to wake up at 5 a.m. for my old job." — Here, the speaker is simply glad things have changed.

Neutral Observation — Sometimes the speaker is not nostalgic or relieved, just simply noting that times have changed.

"Gone are the days when people memorized phone numbers. Now everything is stored in a phone."

So when you hear or read this expression, pay attention to the context. The same structure can express very different feelings.
Real-Life Examples in Full Sentences

Here are some natural, everyday examples that show you how the expression is actually used:

"Gone are the days when you had to go to a travel agent to book a flight. Now you can do it in minutes from your phone."

"Gone are the days of hand-written recipes passed from mother to daughter. Everything is now on the internet."

"He looked at the old neighborhood and sighed. Gone are the days when every door on this street was left unlocked."

"Gone are the days when you could buy a house in the city for a reasonable price."

"Gone are the days of waiting in long queues at the bank — online banking has changed everything."

Notice how each sentence paints a clear contrast between then and now. The expression always implies a "before and after" — a time when something was one way, and a present where it is no longer that way.
What the Expression Is NOT Saying

It is important to understand what this phrase does not mean, so you don't misuse it.

It does not mean that something happened for a very short time. It refers to a whole era or period — a stretch of time during which something was consistently true or common.

It does not always mean forever. Sometimes people use it casually to describe a change in habit or lifestyle, not necessarily a permanent shift in the world.

It is not used for things happening right now or in the future. It is always looking backward.
How Is It Different From Simply Saying "That Doesn't Happen Anymore"?

You could always say, "People don't write letters by hand anymore." That is perfectly clear and correct.

But "Gone are the days when people wrote letters by hand" does something richer. It acknowledges that there was a whole era — a distinct chapter in time — when that was the norm. It gives that past era a sense of weight and significance. It says: "There was a real time when this was a different world, and that world has closed."

This is why the expression feels more emotional and reflective than a plain factual statement. It does not just report a change — it pauses to acknowledge it.
Formal or Informal? Where Will You Hear It?

This expression sits comfortably in both formal and informal settings, though it leans slightly toward the literary or reflective side of language.

You will encounter it in books, novels, and essays. You will hear it in speeches — politicians and leaders often use it to talk about how times have changed. You will find it in journalism, especially in opinion pieces about society and culture. You will also hear it in everyday conversation when someone is feeling nostalgic or reflective.

It is not slang, and it is not overly formal. Think of it as sitting in the comfortable middle ground — expressive and slightly poetic, but not stuffy or academic.
A Useful Variation to Know

You will sometimes hear people say "those were the days" — a related but different expression. While "gone are the days" focuses on the fact that a time has ended, "those were the days" is more purely nostalgic, fondly looking back at good times from the past. They are close cousins but not identical.
A Simple Way to Remember It Forever

Here is a mental image to lock this expression in your memory:

Imagine an old photograph. In it, you can see a moment from the past — people dressed differently, living differently, doing things in a way no one does anymore. You hold that photograph and say: "Gone are the days when life looked like this."

The photograph is the past. The fading of it is the "gone." And the expression is your way of holding both feelings at once — the recognition that time has moved on, and the acknowledgment that it once was a certain way.

In one sentence: "Gone are the days" is an expression that means a particular time or situation from the past no longer exists today — used to reflect on how much things have changed, with a tone that can be nostalgic, relieved, or simply observational.
7092: "Goo-goo" as an adjective describes two closely related things: a look of silly, dreamy infatuation, and anything resembling the soft, meaningless sounds a baby makes. Both meanings share the same feeling — something unguarded, sweet, and a little silly.
Meaning 1: Lovesick and Adoring (The Main Use)

This is by far the most common adjectival use of the word. When you describe someone's eyes or expression as "goo-goo," you mean they are looking at someone with a helplessly adoring, dreamy, starry-eyed gaze — the kind of look that makes it completely obvious that the person is head over heels in love or deeply infatuated.

Think of a teenager who has just fallen for someone and can't stop staring at them with wide, soft, almost glazed eyes. Their expression is melting, tender, and a bit silly — not sharp or composed. That is a goo-goo look.

The most classic phrase: "making goo-goo eyes" — this means gazing at someone with obvious romantic adoration or infatuation, often in a way that others around you can clearly notice (and perhaps find a little embarrassing or amusing).

Examples:

  • "He sat across from her the whole dinner, making goo-goo eyes and barely touching his food."
  • "Stop giving me those goo-goo looks — everyone at the table can see you."
  • "She had a goo-goo expression on her face every time his name came up."

The feeling it carries: It's affectionate but slightly teasing. When you call someone's look "goo-goo," you're acknowledging that their affection is genuine but also that it looks a bit silly or mushy to an outside observer. It's not an insult — it's more of a light, warm, humorous observation. It suggests the person is so smitten that they've lost a little of their composure.

The second meaning connects to the literal sounds babies make — "goo-goo, ga-ga." When used as an adjective in this sense, "goo-goo" describes something that is childlike, babbling, or infantile in nature — speech, behavior, or sounds that resemble what you'd hear from or direct toward a very young baby.

Examples:

  • "She spoke to her puppy in a goo-goo voice, saying things like 'Who's a good boy?'"
  • "The adults started talking in goo-goo tones the moment they saw the newborn."
  • "His goo-goo noises made the baby laugh."

This meaning is often used when adults "baby-talk" — either to actual babies, to pets, or (sometimes playfully) to people they are very fond of. The word captures the soft, cooing, high-pitched, nonsensical quality of that kind of speech.

Both meanings share a common thread: a loss of the normal, composed, "adult" guard. Whether you're gazing adoringly at your crush or cooing at a baby, you're in a state of soft, unguarded, unselfconscious affection. "Goo-goo" captures that sweet, slightly ridiculous loosening of composure that comes with strong tender feeling.

"Goo-goo" is a casual, informal, conversational word. You would use it in everyday speech, friendly writing, or light-hearted contexts. It is not a word you'd find in formal writing or serious situations. It almost always carries a playful or gently teasing tone — even when used affectionately. Nobody says "goo-goo" with a straight, serious face.

It can be used affectionately ("Aww, look at him making goo-goo eyes at her — so cute") or with mild mockery ("Don't go all goo-goo just because he smiled at you"), but in both cases the feeling is light and warm rather than harsh.

UseWhat It MeansTypical Phrase
About a look/expressionDreamy, adoring, lovesick"goo-goo eyes"
About speech/soundsBaby-like, cooing, infantile"goo-goo voice/talk"

In one line: "goo-goo" describes either the helplessly adoring look of someone deeply infatuated, or the soft, babbling, infantile quality of baby-directed speech and sounds. Both uses suggest something sweet, unguarded, and a little silly.
7093: The word goo-goo as a noun has a small cluster of closely related meanings, plus one separate meaning from American political history. Here's everything you need to know.
Meaning 1: The sounds a baby makes

The most basic and widely understood meaning of goo-goo as a noun is the inarticulate, soft, cooing sounds that a very young baby makes — the kind of sounds an infant produces before they can form real words.

When a baby lies on their back and makes that bubbly, rounded, soft vocalization — "gooooo... gaaaa... gooooo" — that is called a goo-goo. These are the first sounds of communication a human being makes, even before babbling proper words.

Example: "She leaned over the crib and smiled at every little goo-goo the baby made."

Because of this association, the word also carries a broader feel of babyish or infantile behaviour. If an adult is being excessively silly, mushy, or childlike around someone they love (especially a romantic partner or a pet), people sometimes say they're "talking goo-goo" or behaving in a goo-goo way.

This is probably the most commonly used noun phrase built from this word. Goo-goo eyes refers to a soft, dreamy, adoring look that someone gives another person when they are infatuated or deeply in love with them.

Imagine someone staring at their crush with wide, melting, almost helpless eyes — lost in admiration, unable to look away, looking slightly dazed and smitten. That expression is goo-goo eyes.

The noun "goo-goo" here captures the idea that love makes people temporarily regress — their gaze becomes as soft and unfocused as a baby's, hence the connection to baby sounds.

Example: "He couldn't stop making goo-goo eyes at her across the dinner table."

The phrase is almost always used in the structure "making goo-goo eyes (at someone)." It has a light, gently teasing tone — people use it to poke fun at someone who is visibly lovestruck.
Meaning 3: A political reformer (historical American English)

This meaning is separate from the baby/love meanings and comes from American political history in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

In this context, a Goo-Goo (often written with capital letters) was a nickname — usually a mocking one — for a member of a "Good Government" reform movement. These were citizens and activists who campaigned against political corruption, especially the corrupt political machines that ran many American cities at the time (such as Tammany Hall in New York City).

The nickname "Goo-Goo" came from the first two syllables of "Good Government" — Goo-Goo is just a shortening of Go-Go-v-ment compressed further: Good Go- → Goo Goo. Politicians who benefited from corruption used this term to mock the reformers as naive, preachy, and unrealistic — basically calling them babies who didn't understand how the real world worked.

Example: "The machine politicians sneered at the Goo-Goos, saying they were dreamers who had never run a real campaign."

Today, this meaning is largely historical. You might encounter it when reading about American political history of that era, but you won't hear it used in everyday modern conversation.

Across its main noun uses, goo-goo always carries a sense of softness, innocence, and something slightly unserious — whether it's a baby's first sounds, the helpless look of someone in love, or (mockingly) a well-meaning idealist in politics. The word itself sounds round and soft on purpose; its sound mimics the feeling it describes.
7094:
A "good egg" is a person who is genuinely kind, honest, trustworthy, and reliable. When you call someone a good egg, you are saying that they have a good character — they are the sort of person who helps others, keeps their word, and can be counted on when it matters.

Think of it this way: if a friend says, "Don't worry about him, he's a good egg," they are reassuring you that this person is decent, well-meaning, and safe to trust.

To understand this idiom, you need to think about eggs.

An egg, from the outside, always looks the same. You cannot tell by looking at the shell whether the egg inside is fresh and good, or rotten and bad. You only find out the truth when you crack it open or when you smell it.

This simple fact gave birth to two powerful expressions:

  • A "bad egg" = an egg that looks fine but is rotten inside → a person who appears respectable but is actually dishonest, corrupt, or untrustworthy. The rottenness is hidden.
  • A "good egg" = an egg that is genuinely fresh and good all the way through → a person who is genuinely good — not just on the surface, but in their true character.

So the idiom is built on this contrast: what something appears to be versus what it truly is. A good egg is the real thing — good through and through.

The expression "bad egg" came first. It appeared in American English around the 1850s, used to describe someone who turned out to be a disappointment or a fraud — a person whose true nature was worse than expected.

"Good egg" followed as the natural opposite. It became especially popular in British slang in the early 1900s, used widely among students, soldiers, and in everyday conversation. It was a warm, friendly way of approving of someone's character.

By the mid-20th century, both expressions had spread across the English-speaking world.
How and When to Use It

Register (how formal it is): "Good egg" is an informal, colloquial expression. You would use it in casual conversation with friends or family, not in a formal report, job application, or official speech.

Tone: The phrase carries a warm, affectionate tone. When you call someone a good egg, it feels friendly and genuine — almost like a hug in words. It is not a cold or neutral compliment; it feels personal.

Who uses it: The phrase is more commonly heard in British English than American English. In Britain, it has a long history and still sounds natural, though it has a slightly old-fashioned or nostalgic flavour today. In America and other parts of the world, people understand it, but it is less commonly used in everyday speech.

When to use it: You use it when you want to vouch for someone's character — to say that a person can be trusted, is kind-hearted, or is just a genuinely decent human being.

Here are several examples so you can see how it works in real conversation:

  1. "You should ask Marcus for help — he's a good egg, he won't let you down."
    (Marcus is reliable and trustworthy.)
  2. "I was nervous about my new neighbour, but she turned out to be a real good egg. She even brought us food when we moved in."
    (The neighbour is kind and generous.)
  3. "Everyone at the office loves her. She's a good egg — always ready to help, never complaining."
    (She has a pleasant, helpful character.)
  4. "My grandfather was a good egg. He never spoke badly of anyone."
    (He was a genuinely decent, virtuous man.)

Notice that in all these examples, the phrase focuses on inner character — kindness, reliability, generosity, honesty — not on talent, skill, or appearance.

It is important to understand what "good egg" does not mean:

  • It does not mean the person is clever or talented. You can call someone a good egg even if they are not particularly smart or skilled.
  • It does not mean the person is famous or successful. A humble, quiet person who simply treats others well is a perfect good egg.
  • It is not a romantic or passionate compliment. It is more of a wholesome, warm approval of someone's everyday decency.

Since "good egg" and "bad egg" are two sides of the same coin, knowing the opposite helps you understand the idiom more deeply.

A "bad egg" is a person who is dishonest, untrustworthy, or morally corrupt — especially someone whose bad character is hidden under a normal appearance. The danger with a bad egg is the deception: they seem fine, but they are not.

Example: "Don't trust him with your money — he's a bad egg. He cheated his own business partner last year."

The contrast makes the meaning of "good egg" even sharper: a good egg is not just someone who seems good — they are good, genuinely, when you get to know them.
A Small Note on Tone in Modern Usage

Today, calling someone a good egg sounds slightly old-fashioned or nostalgic, like something a grandparent might say. This does not make it wrong or incorrect — it just means the phrase carries a gentle, warm, slightly vintage charm. In fact, this quality makes it feel more sincere and heartfelt when you use it, because it does not sound like a cold, modern transaction. It sounds human.

MeaningA genuinely kind, trustworthy, and decent person
OriginFrom the image of a fresh, good egg vs. a rotten one
RegisterInformal and colloquial
ToneWarm, affectionate, sincere
Used most inBritish English, though understood everywhere
Opposite"Bad egg" — a dishonest or corrupt person

In short: if someone calls you a good egg, take it as a lovely compliment. It means they see you as a truly good person — not just someone who acts good when others are watching, but someone whose goodness is real, reliable, and runs all the way through.
7095:
"Good grief!" is an exclamation — something you say out loud as a sudden, spontaneous reaction to something. It expresses emotions like surprise, shock, frustration, disbelief, or exasperation (that feeling of "I can't believe this is happening again").

Think of it as a slightly old-fashioned but still widely understood way of saying things like:

  • "Oh my God!"
  • "Oh wow, seriously?!"
  • "I can't believe it!"
  • "Are you kidding me?!"

Here's the important thing: it is mild and inoffensive. Unlike many strong exclamations in English, "good grief!" is perfectly safe to say around children, elders, coworkers, or anyone. It carries emotional weight without being rude or vulgar.
Why Do the Words Seem to Contradict Each Other?

If you look at the two words individually, they seem to make no sense together. "Good" is positive. "Grief" means deep sadness or suffering. So why would sadness be good?

The answer is that you should never try to understand this idiom word by word. The phrase works as a whole unit — the individual words have essentially lost their literal meanings. This is true of many idioms in every language.

But there is a logical history behind the phrase, and understanding it will help you remember it forever.
The Origin: What Is a "Minced Oath"?

"Good grief!" belongs to a category of expressions called minced oaths.

A minced oath is a softened or "watered-down" substitute for a stronger, more offensive expression — often a religious one. Historically, in English-speaking Christian cultures, using the name of God casually as an exclamation (like "Good God!") was considered disrespectful, even sinful. So people cleverly replaced the offensive word with a similar-sounding or emotionally equivalent word that wouldn't offend anyone.

"Good grief!" is widely believed to be a softened form of "Good God!" The word "grief" was substituted for "God" to keep the same emotional punch while removing the potential offense.

This is a very common pattern in English. Here are other examples of minced oaths you may have heard:

  • "Gosh!" → softened form of "God!"
  • "Gee!" or "Jeez!" → softened form of "Jesus!"
  • "Good gracious!" → softened form of "Good God!"
  • "Good heavens!" → softened form of "Good God!"
  • "Darn!" → softened form of "Damn!"
  • "Shoot!" → softened form of a much stronger word

So "good grief" fits perfectly into this family. It was born out of politeness and social caution, and it stuck around because it works — it sounds natural, it's easy to say quickly, and it conveys exactly the right emotional energy.

"Good grief!" is emotionally versatile. The specific feeling it expresses depends on the situation and the tone of voice. Here are the main emotions it can carry:

1. Surprise or shock
When something catches you completely off guard.

"Good grief! You finished the whole project in one day?"

2. Frustration
When something is annoying or not going the way it should.

"Good grief, the Wi-Fi is down again!"

3. Exasperation
That specific feeling of being worn out because something keeps happening.

"Good grief, this is the third time this week I've been late!"

4. Disbelief
When something seems so strange or extreme that it's hard to accept.

"Good grief! That tiny apartment costs $4,000 a month?!"

5. Mild alarm or dismay
When you notice something that concerns or upsets you.

"Good grief, look at the mess in here!"

Notice that in all these cases, the emotion is reactive — something just happened, and "good grief!" is your immediate, instinctive response to it.

Many learners hear the word "grief" and think this phrase must relate to literal grief — mourning someone who died, or deep sadness. This is incorrect.

"Good grief!" is almost never used in a situation involving actual loss, death, or serious emotional pain. You would not say "good grief" when someone tells you a loved one has passed away — that would be strange and inappropriate.

The word "grief" here is a fossil. It's just a leftover from the historical substitution explained earlier, and it no longer carries its original meaning inside this phrase. Remember: idioms are not built from the sum of their parts.
Grammar and Usage: How to Use It Correctly

1. It almost always stands alone as an exclamation.
It typically appears at the very beginning of a sentence, followed by a comma or exclamation mark, and then the rest of your thought:

"Good grief, I forgot my umbrella again!"
"Good grief! How did you manage to do that?"

Or it can stand entirely on its own as a complete utterance:

— "The flight is delayed by six hours."
— "Good grief!"

2. It is not usually split or modified.
You would not say "very good grief" or "such good grief." The phrase is fixed. Use it exactly as it is.

3. Capitalization and punctuation.
When written, it often starts with a capital "G" because it begins a sentence or stands alone. It's almost always followed by an exclamation mark (!), which reflects the emotional energy it carries. A period would make it feel flat and unnatural.

4. Tone of voice matters.
In speech, you can shift the meaning slightly by changing your tone:

  • Said with rising pitch and wide eyes → pure surprise
  • Said slowly with a sigh → exhaustion and exasperation
  • Said sharply → frustration or mild anger
Formality Level: Where Can You Use It?

"Good grief!" sits comfortably in informal to semi-informal settings. It's perfectly appropriate:

  • In casual conversation with friends and family
  • In the workplace (it's not edgy or risky)
  • Around children (it's completely clean)
  • In everyday writing, like a text message or casual email

It would feel slightly out of place in a very formal speech, an academic paper, or professional writing — but only because exclamations like this generally don't belong in those contexts, not because "good grief" is considered improper.

The most famous user of "good grief!" in popular culture is Charlie Brown, the beloved cartoon character from the American comic strip Peanuts, created by Charles M. Schulz (which ran from 1950 to 2000, and remains hugely popular worldwide). Charlie Brown says "Good grief!" so frequently that it became his signature catchphrase.

He usually says it when things go wrong for him — missing a football kick, failing at something he tried hard to do, or dealing with frustrating situations. This association helped make the phrase universally recognizable, especially in American culture. Even people who aren't native English speakers often know "good grief!" because of Charlie Brown.

"Good grief!" is still understood by virtually all English speakers, though it's used more often by older generations. Younger speakers are more likely to use "Oh my God!" or "Are you serious?!" in the same situations. However, "good grief" is not considered outdated or strange — it's simply a choice with a slightly classic, wholesome feel to it. Using it will make you sound natural and even charming.

• What it is: An exclamation (something you say as a sudden emotional reaction).
  • What it expresses: Surprise, frustration, disbelief, exasperation, or mild shock.
  • What it does NOT mean: Actual grief or sadness in the literal sense.
  • Why "good" + "grief"? It's a minced oath — a polished-up substitute for "Good God!" created to avoid religious offense.
  • Is it rude? Not at all. It's mild, clean, and appropriate almost everywhere.
  • How to use it: As a standalone exclamation or at the start of a sentence, followed by an exclamation mark.
  • Famous for: Being Charlie Brown's go-to catchphrase in Peanuts.
  • Key rule: Never interpret the words individually. Treat the whole phrase as one single unit of meaning.

Before you learn the meaning of this term in diplomacy and international law, you need to understand the word offices as it is used here. In modern English, "offices" usually means a place where people work. But the word has an older meaning that survives in formal and legal language: services, acts, or functions performed on behalf of someone. Think of the phrase "through the offices of a friend," which means "through the help or efforts of a friend."

So good offices literally means good or helpful services — specifically, services rendered by a neutral party to help two quarreling parties come together.

Good offices is a method used in international diplomacy and international law where a neutral third party — a country, an international organization, or a respected individual — steps in to help two parties who are in conflict to start talking to each other, usually when those two parties are unable or unwilling to communicate directly.

The key idea is simple: the third party does not try to solve the dispute, does not propose solutions, and does not make any decisions. Their only job is to act as a bridge — to open communication channels, reduce tension, persuade the parties to meet, and get negotiations started. Once the parties are talking, the role of good offices is essentially done.

Think of it this way: imagine two neighbors who have had a bitter fight and refuse to look at each other. A mutual friend comes to both of them separately, says kind words, cools down tempers, and convinces both to sit at the same table. That mutual friend is offering good offices. They are not a judge. They are not deciding who is right. They are simply bringing people to the table.

In the world of international relations, disputes between countries can arise all the time — over borders, treaties, trade, or military actions. Ideally, countries should settle their disputes peacefully. But there is a problem: sometimes two parties in a dispute are so hostile to each other, or so politically embarrassed, that they cannot be seen talking directly to one another. A direct meeting might look like weakness to their own citizens. Or, communication may have completely broken down due to war or severed diplomatic ties.

This is precisely where good offices becomes valuable. A neutral third party provides both sides with a face-saving way to begin dialogue without anyone having to publicly admit they want to negotiate. The third party makes the first moves quietly, behind the scenes.

Good offices is usually informal and flexible. There is no strict procedure. The third party who offers good offices typically does one or more of the following:

First, they approach each of the disputing parties privately and separately, listening to their concerns and signaling willingness to help. This is sometimes called "shuttle diplomacy" — going back and forth between the parties.

Second, they may transmit messages, communications, or proposals between the two sides when the parties refuse to communicate directly, acting essentially as a trusted messenger.

Third, they may provide a neutral venue — a location, a building, or even a country — where the two parties can eventually meet without it being seen as one side going to the other's territory (which would itself be a political statement).

Fourth, they work to reduce hostility and create the right atmosphere for dialogue — lowering the emotional temperature, so to speak.

Crucially, the third party offering good offices has no authority to impose anything. Their involvement is only as strong as both parties allow it to be. Either side can reject the offer of good offices at any time, and the third party cannot force the issue. The moment both parties are willing to talk directly, the role of good offices fades into the background.

The concept of good offices was formally recognized in international law in the Hague Convention for the Pacific Settlement of International Disputes, first adopted in 1899 and revised in 1907. These landmark agreements were part of a broader effort to reduce war by establishing peaceful methods of dispute resolution.

The Hague Conventions explicitly distinguished good offices from other methods and stated that the offer of good offices is never to be considered an unfriendly act — meaning that if a third country offers to help, neither of the disputing parties should take offense at the gesture. This was important because, without such a rule, an offer of help could be misread as interference or as taking sides.

Today, good offices is recognized as one of several methods of peaceful dispute settlement listed in Article 33 of the United Nations Charter, which calls on parties to any dispute to seek solutions through negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement, or other peaceful means — good offices falling within that broader umbrella of peaceful diplomatic tools.

Almost anyone with the trust of both parties and the standing to act can offer good offices. In practice, good offices are offered by:

States (Countries): A neutral country that is not involved in the dispute can offer its services. Switzerland, for example, has a long tradition of offering good offices because of its historical neutrality. Sweden has similarly played this role in various international conflicts.

International Organizations: The United Nations — particularly the UN Secretary-General — frequently offers good offices to help resolve conflicts around the world. This is one of the most important functions of the office of the Secretary-General. The Secretary-General's good offices can involve sending a personal envoy, making direct appeals to leaders, or facilitating quiet diplomatic conversations.

Individual Persons: A respected and trusted individual — a former head of state, a senior diplomat, or a well-regarded statesperson — can also be asked or can volunteer to offer good offices. Former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, for instance, was appointed as a joint UN-Arab League envoy to Syria in 2012, a role rooted in the tradition of personal good offices.
Real Examples to Cement the Idea

Norway and the Oslo Accords (1993): The talks that led to the historic Oslo Accords between Israel and the PLO (Palestine Liberation Organization) began with Norway offering good offices. Norwegian diplomats quietly facilitated secret meetings between Israeli and Palestinian negotiators in Norway, providing a neutral location, keeping the talks confidential, and enabling communication when public negotiations seemed impossible. Norway did not dictate the terms — it simply made the conversation possible.

Switzerland as a Protecting Power: When two countries sever diplomatic relations (i.e., close their embassies and stop talking), they often ask a neutral country to act as a "protecting power" and represent their interests. Switzerland has historically taken on this role between countries like the United States and Iran, effectively offering a form of good offices by maintaining a channel of communication.

UN Secretary-General's Good Offices: The UN Secretary-General has offered good offices in dozens of conflicts — from Cyprus to Afghanistan to Guatemala. The Secretary-General may send a personal representative to a conflict zone to speak with both sides, or may personally telephone heads of state to push for dialogue. This is classic good offices: facilitating without deciding.
The Critical Distinction: Good Offices vs. Similar Methods

Since good offices exists alongside other methods of peaceful dispute settlement, it's important to understand exactly how it differs from them, because learners often confuse these terms.

Good Offices vs. Mediation: This is the most common point of confusion. Both involve a neutral third party. The difference lies in how active that third party is. In good offices, the third party only helps the disputing sides to begin communicating — they do not actively participate in the substance of negotiations and do not propose solutions. In mediation, the third party goes much further: they actively participate in the negotiations, help the parties explore solutions, and often propose a settlement themselves. Mediation is a deeper, more hands-on involvement. Good offices, in a sense, paves the way for mediation or direct negotiation — it is often the first step before more formal processes begin.

Good Offices vs. Conciliation: Conciliation is even more formal than mediation. A conciliator typically conducts an investigation, examines the facts and legal issues of the dispute, and produces a formal report with recommendations for how the dispute should be settled, though those recommendations are still not legally binding. Good offices involves none of this — no investigation, no report, no recommendations.

Good Offices vs. Arbitration/Judicial Settlement: These are fully formal legal processes where a court or arbitral tribunal examines the dispute and issues a legally binding decision. Good offices is entirely different in nature — it is non-binding, informal, and focused on facilitating dialogue rather than delivering a verdict.

In short, you can think of these methods as existing on a spectrum from least formal to most formal: Good Offices → Mediation → Conciliation → Arbitration → Judicial Settlement.

To sharpen your understanding, it helps to know what good offices specifically excludes:

  • It is not interference in another country's internal affairs, even though a third party is getting involved. International law recognizes good offices as a legitimate and friendly act.
  • It is not a guarantee of peace. The third party cannot force either side to keep talking or to reach an agreement.
  • It is not legally binding in any way. Nothing the third party does during good offices creates legal obligations for the disputing parties.
  • It is not a judgment on who is right or wrong. The third party takes no position on the merits of the dispute.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Good offices is a peaceful, non-binding, and informal diplomatic method where a neutral third party — a state, an international organization, or an individual — helps two disputing parties open a channel of communication and begin talks, without participating in those talks itself or proposing solutions. Its sole purpose is to get the parties to the table. It is the gentlest and most preliminary form of third-party assistance in international dispute resolution, legally recognized since the Hague Conventions of 1899 and frequently used by the United Nations today. It is distinct from mediation (where the third party proposes solutions), conciliation (which involves investigation and formal recommendations), and arbitration or judicial settlement (which produce binding decisions).

When you see the phrase "good offices" in a diplomatic news report or a legal document, you now know it always means: a neutral party is helping hostile parties talk — nothing more, and nothing less.
7097:
"Good riddance" is something you say when you are happy and relieved that someone or something is finally gone.

The key feeling here is relief mixed with a little satisfaction. You're not just saying "that thing is gone." You're saying "that thing is gone, and honestly? Thank goodness for that."

Think of it this way: imagine you had a leaking, smelly old bag that you had been carrying for miles. When you finally throw it away, you sigh with relief and think, "I'm so glad I don't have to carry that anymore." That feeling — that sigh of relief about something or someone leaving — is exactly what "good riddance" expresses.

The word riddance comes from the verb "to rid", which means to free yourself from something unwanted or troublesome. When you "get rid of" something, you remove it from your life. Riddance is simply the noun form of that action — the act of getting rid of something.

So "good riddance" literally means: "It is a good thing that we have been freed from this."

The complete, original form of this idiom is:

"Good riddance to bad rubbish."

This longer version makes the meaning even clearer. It says: "It's a good thing that this bad, worthless thing (or person) is gone — just like throwing out garbage." Over time, people started dropping the second part and just saying "good riddance", but the full meaning stayed the same.

"Good riddance" is not a neutral or polite expression. It carries a strong emotional charge. When you use it, you are making it clear that:

  • The person or thing that left was unpleasant, troublesome, or unwanted.
  • You feel no sadness about their departure.
  • In fact, you feel relieved or even glad they are gone.

This makes it a somewhat blunt and harsh phrase. It's perfectly fine to say it privately among close friends, or even out loud when you're venting. But you wouldn't typically say it to someone's face, because it is essentially telling them: "I'm happy you're leaving." That would be quite rude in most social situations.

You can use "good riddance" in three main situations:

1. When a difficult person leaves
If a rude coworker quits, or a toxic friend walks out of your life, or a bad boss finally retires, you might say: "Good riddance."

2. When a bad situation ends
If a long, painful project is finally over, or a difficult period in your life comes to an end, you might say: "Good riddance to all of that stress."

3. When an annoying thing is gone
If your old, constantly-breaking-down car is finally scrapped, or your noisy, malfunctioning computer is replaced, you might say: "Good riddance to that piece of junk."

Here are some natural, realistic examples to show you how people use this idiom:

  • Her overbearing boss finally resigned. She whispered to her friend, "Good riddance."
  • After years of dealing with a noisy, rude neighbor who finally moved away, her father said, "Good riddance to bad rubbish."
  • The old, broken-down bus was taken out of service. The regular passengers joked among themselves: "Good riddance — that thing broke down every other week."
  • After a painful, drawn-out legal dispute was finally settled and over, he leaned back in his chair and said, "Good riddance. I never want to go through that again."
  • When winter finally ended after months of freezing cold, she opened her window, took a deep breath of warm spring air, and said, "Good riddance, winter!"

It's important to know what this phrase does not mean, so you don't misuse it:

  • It does not mean "goodbye" in a normal, neutral way. A regular goodbye expresses farewell with no strong judgment. "Good riddance" carries a clear negative judgment about the person or thing leaving.
  • It does not mean you are simply indifferent to someone leaving. Indifference is "I don't care." Good riddance goes a step further — it means you are actively glad they are gone.
  • It does not have to be said to the person leaving. In fact, it's most commonly said after they've gone, or to someone else, as a commentary.

"Good riddance" is what you say when something or someone unwanted, troublesome, or unpleasant finally leaves your life — and you feel relieved and glad about it. It's honest, a little sharp, and carries the quiet satisfaction of finally being free from something that was weighing you down. Think of it as the verbal equivalent of washing your hands and walking away from something you never wanted to deal with in the first place.

A "good Samaritan" is a person who helps a stranger in need, without expecting anything in return — not money, not praise, not a favour back. The help is purely out of kindness and compassion.

You might hear it used like this: "A good Samaritan stopped on the highway to help when my car broke down." That just means a kind stranger helped someone they had no obligation to help.
Where Did the Term Come From?

The phrase comes from a story (called a parable) told by Jesus in the Bible, found in the Gospel of Luke (Chapter 10, verses 25–37). It is one of the most famous stories ever told, and understanding it properly is the key to understanding the term.

The Story, Told Simply:

A man is travelling alone on a road from Jerusalem to Jericho. This road was notorious for being dangerous — robbers frequently attacked travellers on it.

Sure enough, robbers attack him. They beat him, steal everything he has, and leave him half-dead by the side of the road.

Three people come along, one by one:

  1. A Priest — a religious leader, someone you'd expect to be moral and caring. He sees the wounded man... and crosses to the other side of the road to avoid him.
  2. A Levite — another respected religious figure in Jewish society. He also comes close, takes a look at the wounded man... and also walks away.
  3. A Samaritan — and here is where the story becomes shocking to its original audience.

To understand the power of the story, you need to understand who Samaritans were.

Samaritans were a group of people who lived in a region called Samaria, between Jerusalem and Galilee. Jews and Samaritans deeply despised each other. The hatred between them was centuries old, rooted in racial, cultural, and religious differences. To a Jewish person of that era, a Samaritan was an outsider, an enemy, someone "less than." The feeling was mutual — Samaritans disliked Jews equally.

So in the original story, the man who was beaten was almost certainly Jewish. The audience listening to Jesus tell this story was also Jewish. When they heard "a Samaritan came along," they fully expected him to be the villain, or at best, to ignore the man just like the others.

Instead, the Samaritan does the opposite of what everyone expected.

The Samaritan:

  • Stopped, even though he was travelling and had no obligation whatsoever to help an enemy.
  • Felt compassion — the Bible says he was moved with pity when he saw the man.
  • Cleaned and bandaged his wounds, using oil and wine (which were used medicinally at the time).
  • Lifted the man onto his own donkey and walked beside him to the nearest inn.
  • Paid the innkeeper to take care of the man, out of his own pocket.
  • Promised to pay any extra costs on his way back if the man needed more care.

He gave his time, his supplies, his money, and his effort — all for a stranger from a group that looked down on his own people.
The Deeper Point of the Story

Jesus told this parable in response to a question: "Who is my neighbour?" The idea of "loving your neighbour" was an established moral principle, but the questioner wanted to know — who exactly counts as a neighbour? Just the people who look like you? People in your community?

The parable's answer is radical and clear: your neighbour is whoever needs your help, regardless of who they are. And more importantly — being a "good neighbour" is about what you do, not who you are.

The two people who walked away (the Priest and the Levite) were the "respectable" ones. The one who actually helped was the "enemy." The story flips every expectation upside down on purpose.
How the Term Is Used Today

Over time, this Biblical story became so well-known that it entered everyday language. Today, you don't have to be religious or even know the original story to use the term. It is used in three main contexts:

1. In Everyday Speech

Calling someone a "good Samaritan" simply means they are a kind stranger who helped someone without being asked and without expecting anything back.

Examples:

  • "A good Samaritan returned my lost wallet with all the cash still inside."
  • "Good Samaritans formed a human chain to rescue the swimmer from the rip current."

2. As a General Personality Description

If you call someone "a real good Samaritan," you're saying they are the kind of person who habitually goes out of their way to help others — a genuinely selfless, compassionate individual.

3. In Law — "Good Samaritan Laws"

Many countries have laws named after this term. Good Samaritan laws are legal protections for people who voluntarily help someone in an emergency. The purpose is to encourage bystanders to help — without fear that they'll be sued or face legal trouble if something goes wrong while they were trying to help in good faith.

For example: If you see someone collapse on the street, attempt CPR, and accidentally break a rib (which can happen), a Good Samaritan law would protect you from being sued for that injury, because you were genuinely trying to help.

These laws exist in the USA, Canada, Australia, the UK, and many other countries, though the exact protections vary.

To be called a good Samaritan, a person's action typically involves all of these:

  • Helping a stranger — not a friend or family member (helping them is just expected)
  • No obligation — they didn't have to help, but they chose to
  • No personal gain — they didn't do it for money, fame, or a favour in return
  • Real, practical help — actual action, not just sympathy
  • Often at a personal cost — their own time, energy, money, or safety

It's worth being clear about what the term doesn't mean:

  • It doesn't mean simply being a nice person in general.
  • It doesn't apply to professionals doing their job (a paramedic helping someone isn't a good Samaritan — that's their duty).
  • It isn't about donating to charity (though that's kind, it doesn't quite fit the term).
  • It isn't used when someone has a personal reason or incentive to help.

The heart of the term is unexpected, selfless help for a stranger in a moment of need.

ConceptSimple Explanation

The term "good Samaritan" means a kind stranger who steps up to help someone in need, with no obligation and no expectation of reward. It comes from a 2,000-year-old Biblical story where the person least expected to help — a Samaritan, historically an enemy of the victim — turned out to be the only one who actually did. Today, the phrase is used in everyday conversation, as a personality compliment, and even in legal language to protect people who help others in emergencies. Its core message is timeless: true compassion doesn't check who someone is before deciding to help.
7099:
Good-natured describes a person who has a naturally kind, cheerful, and pleasant disposition. It means they are consistently friendly, easy to get along with, and not easily upset, angered, or irritated — and crucially, this isn't something they have to try hard at. It comes from within. It is simply who they are.

The word is built on the idea of one's nature — your natural inner personality and temperament. A good-natured person's default setting is warmth, patience, and pleasantness.

Think of the most easygoing, warm person you know — the one who always seems relaxed and cheerful, who makes everyone feel comfortable, who laughs things off rather than brooding, who rarely snaps or complains even when things go wrong. That person is almost certainly good-natured.

In everyday life, a good-natured person stays calm and pleasant even in mildly frustrating situations. When someone teases or jokes with them, they laugh along instead of taking offense. When others make mistakes, they respond with patience rather than criticism. They don't hold grudges. They don't have a short fuse. Being around them just feels easy.
It Describes a Consistent Trait, Not a Moment

This is an important nuance. Good-natured refers to a person's overall temperament — something stable and reliable about who they are, not a one-time act of kindness or a good mood on a particular day. You wouldn't call someone good-natured just because they smiled at you once. It means they are reliably and consistently warm, pleasant, and cheerful across situations and over time.
It Can Describe More Than Just People

While most commonly used for people, good-natured can also describe behaviors, remarks, laughter, or interactions:

"Good-natured teasing" means playful, friendly joking that isn't meant to hurt anyone. "Good-natured laughter" is warm laughter that includes everyone rather than mocking someone. "A good-natured debate" is one where both sides stay friendly and light, without hostility.

In all these cases, the word signals that something was done in a warm, friendly, non-hostile spirit.

Good-natured does not mean weak or a pushover. A good-natured person can absolutely stand their ground and express disagreement — they just do so without being harsh, cold, or hostile.

It does not mean fake niceness. Someone who performs pleasantness for social reasons but secretly resents everything is not good-natured. True good-naturedness is genuine — it comes from within, not from strategy.

It also does not mean naive or gullible. Being cheerful and warm has nothing to do with being easily fooled.

• "Even after the long delay, she remained good-natured and kept the conversation light."
  • "He's so good-natured that even when people tease him, he just laughs along."
  • "The teacher's good-natured humor made the class feel relaxed and enjoyable."
  • "It was just good-natured banter between old friends — nobody meant any harm."
  • "What I admire most about him is his good-natured patience; nothing seems to rattle him for long."
How It Compares to Similar Words

Amiable is very close in meaning, but it focuses more specifically on being likable and friendly in social situations — it emphasizes how well someone gets along with others. Good-natured is broader and includes the idea of emotional steadiness and cheerfulness.

Affable means easy and pleasant to talk to. It highlights approachability. Good-natured includes that, but also the idea of not getting easily upset.

Genial means warm and cheerful in a sociable way — very similar to good-natured, but genial is often used in more formal or literary contexts.

Easygoing means relaxed and unbothered. It overlaps significantly with good-natured but focuses more on being laid-back and stress-free, while good-natured also carries warmth and kindness.

Pleasant simply means agreeable or enjoyable. It's more general and doesn't carry the deeper idea of a stable inner temperament.

Of all these, good-natured is the richest because it captures the whole package — kindness, cheerfulness, patience, and emotional warmth — all rooted in who a person naturally is at their core.

If you had to remember just one thing: a good-natured person is someone whose natural, default personality is warm, cheerful, patient, and easy to be around — and who stays that way without much effort, because that's simply who they are.
